Part Two · The fix nobody noticed

The Quiet Chip

American car theft fell eighty percent and stayed down for thirty years. It was not policing, prison, demographics or the economy. It was a component with no battery, no moving parts, and no sound.

By Oliver Bacon · 13 minute read

Part One ended on a puzzle. A century of locks, sirens and steel bars mostly moved car theft around rather than reducing it — and yet the reduction, when it finally came, was one of the largest declines in any category of crime ever recorded in the United States.

Between 1990 and 2020 the American vehicle theft rate fell by eighty percent. Not a dip. Not a trend. A structural collapse, sustained across three decades, four presidencies, two recessions and an entire rebuild of American policing.

And here is the genuinely startling part, which is the opening premise of the most thorough study yet published on the subject: for most of that period, nobody could satisfactorily explain it.

“The vehicle theft rate in the United States declined 80 percent between 1990 and 2020. Remarkably, this remains unexplained.”
Graham Farrell, The great American car crime decline, 2025
Fig. 1US vehicle thefts, selected years, 1960–2025

Plotted through sourced anchor years, not a complete annual series — the shape is reliable, the intermediate years are interpolated between marked points. 1991 peak and 2025 total are exact. The shaded band marks the period across which electronic immobilizers spread through the American fleet.

One

What came before, and why it wore off

The United States had tried legislating vehicle security before, and it had worked — temporarily. Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 114, from 1968, required better door locks, the buzzer that nags when you leave the key in, and ignition locks that prevent a car being steered or driven with the key removed. Manufacturers met it by 1969.

Evaluations credit that rule with the roughly one-third decline in vehicle theft across the 1970s. It brought the problem, in one researcher's phrase, under control for lengthy periods. Then it wore off — not because the locks stopped working, but because thieves learned to go around them. By the mid-eighties one study estimated that as much as eighty percent of vehicle theft was being accomplished by a single technique: breaking the steering column shroud and forcing the mechanism with a large screwdriver. The trade called it peeling the column.

This is the pattern that makes vehicle security genuinely interesting as a subject. It is not a fixed problem with a fixed answer. It is an arms race, and every measure has a half-life.

Two

A law about stencils

What eventually broke the cycle began as legislation aimed at something else entirely.

The Motor Vehicle Theft Law Enforcement Act was introduced to Congress in 1978 and reintroduced every year until it finally passed in 1984. Its formal emphasis was parts marking — stamping identification numbers onto major components of high-theft models so that chop shops could not launder them. That was the headline, and it consumed most of the evaluation effort that followed.

The evaluations of parts marking came back equivocal at best. But the Act did something more consequential almost as a side effect: it created a regulatory incentive for manufacturers to improve security specifically on their highest-risk vehicles, or face the marking requirement. Fit better security, and a model could be exempted.

General Motors took the deal. In 1986 it introduced the PASS-Key system, and it fitted it first to precisely the two cars that needed it most — the Pontiac Firebird and the Chevrolet Camaro, which were the two highest-theft models of 1985.

This turns out to be the single luckiest fact in the entire history of crime prevention research. Because by fitting the new system to some models and not others, in the same year, from the same manufacturer, with no other design changes, General Motors accidentally built a controlled experiment.

Three

How the handshake works

Before the immobilizer, starting a car was a purely mechanical proposition. The key cylinder completed a circuit. Anything else that completed the same circuit — a screwdriver, two stripped wires, a slide hammer — started the car just as well.

The immobilizer inserts a conversation into that process. Embedded in the key is a passive transponder: an RFID chip with no battery, powered entirely by the field the car generates when the key comes near. The car asks a question. The chip answers with a code. If the answer is wrong, or there is no answer at all, the engine control unit declines to enable the fuel pump, the ignition, or the starter.

Fig. 2The exchange that ended hot-wiring

The critical property is that it is passive. The driver does nothing, remembers nothing, and arms nothing. Unlike every deterrent in Part One, an immobilizer cannot be forgotten, cannot be left off, and never cries wolf.

A thief can still peel the column. They can still hot-wire it perfectly. The car simply will not go, because the part being defeated is no longer the part in charge.

Four

The cliff edge

Farrell's study reconstructs the GM natural experiment from industry data filed in the Federal Register and from successive NHTSA reports to Congress, comparing the models that received PASS-Key against a matched control group of similar vehicles that did not — the Firebird and Camaro against other sporty models including the Ford Mustang.

−80%Theft of immobilizer-equipped models vs matched controls
1986GM fits PASS-Key to the Firebird and Camaro
54% → 22%GM's share of new-vehicle thefts, 1985 to 1995
1991The year American car theft peaked and turned

The size of the drop is not the most persuasive part. The shape is. It is not a gentle improvement consistent with better policing or a stronger economy; it is a cliff edge, appearing exactly where the technology appears, in the models that got it, and not in the ones that didn't.

In 1985 General Motors accounted for 41 percent of American production and 54 percent of thefts. By 1995, with immobilizers standard across its high-risk models, it accounted for 31 percent of production and 22 percent of thefts. The company had not become less desirable. It had become harder.

And the reason the national decline took three decades rather than three years is simply fleet turnover. An immobilizer only protects the car it is fitted to. The national rate could only fall as fast as secure vehicles replaced insecure ones — which is also why theft of new vehicles fell before theft of older ones, precisely as the theory predicts and precisely as the data shows.

Five

Five countries, one pattern

If the immobilizer really is the cause, then the same fingerprint should appear in every country that adopted it — at a different date in each, matching that country's own rollout rather than any shared global trend. It does.

Fig. 3When immobilizers arrived — and when theft turned

Every peak follows its own country's rollout, not a global calendar. Note also that fitting consistently begins before any legal mandate — manufacturers moved in anticipation of legislation, which is why several national declines appear to start “too early” to be credited to the law that supposedly caused them.

The Netherlands is the cleanest case. Fitting began around 1990; by 1995 roughly one car in five had a factory immobilizer. Dutch theft peaked in 1995 and had fallen 85 percent by 2008. Had immobilizers genuinely arrived only with the European mandate, that peak is too early, the turn too sharp, and the decline too steep for the number of secure cars on the road.

Australia mandated them for new vehicles in 2001, and Australian theft peaked in 2001 — but 27 percent of the fleet already had one by 2000, rising to 65 percent by 2004. Canada mandated them in 2007, having already seen declines begin earlier, with Winnipeg — long the country's car theft capital — fitting them years ahead of the national requirement. Across the European Union, Directive 95/56 came into force in 1998.

The United States, notably, never mandated anything. It got there first anyway, in 1986, because a law about stencils made it commercially rational for General Motors to fit one.

Six

The control group nobody meant to run

Scientifically, the immobilizer thesis had one gap: no modern manufacturer would ever be reckless enough to sell a large volume of cars without one, so there was no contemporary control group.

Then two of them did exactly that.

Certain base-model Hyundai and Kia vehicles sold in the United States were built without engine immobilizers long after the technology was standard almost everywhere else. For years this was an obscure specification footnote. Then, in 2022, the method for exploiting it — strip the column, and turn the exposed ignition with the metal shell of a USB cable — spread across social media, and the results were immediate and enormous.

Nineteen-eighties theft techniques worked perfectly on cars built in the twenty-tens, for one reason and one reason only.The exception that proves the rule

This is as close to a controlled trial as criminology is ever likely to get. Same era, same roads, same policing, same economy, same insurance market. The variable was a component costing a few dollars, and its absence was worth a national crime wave. American theft totals climbed back over a million by 2023 — a figure last seen in the 1990s.

And then the correction arrived just as sharply, once the manufacturers issued software immobilizer updates, distributed steering-wheel locks, and law enforcement organized around it. Thefts fell 17 percent in 2024 and a further 23 percent in 2025, landing at 659,880 — the lowest figure in decades.

Two enormous, opposite movements in three years, both traceable to the presence or absence of the same chip.

Seven

What thieves did instead

Crime prevention rarely eliminates offenders. It reprices the work. And having made hot-wiring pointless, the immobilizer pushed vehicle theft in three directions, all of which require something the 1980s thief never needed: either a computer, or the actual key.

Relay attacks. Keyless-entry cars are looking for their fob continuously. Two people with signal amplifiers — one near the house, one near the car — can capture the fob's signal through a front door and relay it to the vehicle, which concludes the owner is standing beside it. Nothing is broken and nothing is hacked. The car's own logic is used correctly, on a lie about distance.

Port programming. Break in, plug a handheld unit into the diagnostic port under the dash, and program a fresh key on the spot. The car then accepts the new key as legitimate, because as far as the car is concerned, it is.

Simply taking the keys. The bleakest consequence of good security is that it makes the owner the weakest component. When bypassing the electronics is hard, home burglary and carjacking become comparatively attractive — a genuine and under-discussed cost of the technology's success.

Fig. 4What actually protects a car, against what it costs you

Positions are editorial judgment, informed by the evidence in these two articles rather than a single measured dataset. The pattern worth noting is the top-left corner: the things that work best are the things that ask nothing of you, which is exactly why they work.

Eight

Is old technology safer now?

There is a real question buried in all this, and it is the same question as choosing a typewriter over email because a typewriter cannot be subpoenaed from a server. If modern theft is fundamentally digital, is an older, dumber car actually harder to steal?

Mostly, no — and the Kia and Hyundai episode is the proof. A car with no immobilizer is vulnerable to a technique from 1985 that requires no equipment, no skill and no computer. Analog is not the same as secure.

But there is one exception, and it is the best joke in the entire subject.

The most effective anti-theft device available on a modern car is a manual transmission. Not because it is clever — because it is unfamiliar. A thief who cannot drive a stick cannot steal a stick, and there are documented cases of attempted thefts collapsing in exactly that fashion, sometimes noisily, in the owner's driveway. It is not marketed as security. It costs nothing. It cannot be relayed, cloned, hacked or amplified. And its effectiveness is rising every year, purely because fewer people can operate one.

It is the only security feature that gets stronger the more obsolete it becomes.The third pedal

Which brings the two halves of this story back together. Part One was full of deterrents that shouted — sirens, steel bars, flashing lights, all of them advertising their own presence and most of them failing. The thing that actually worked said nothing at all. It sat inside the key, drew no power, made no noise, demanded nothing of the owner, and quietly declined to start the car.

Farrell's paper closes on a claim that sounds like overreach until you have followed the evidence to it: if this technology also suppressed the wider crime drop that followed — and the collapse in vehicle theft removed a whole apprenticeship route into other offending — then the electronic engine immobilizer may be the most important crime prevention device of recent history.

Not the alarm. Not the Club. A grain of rice in a plastic key, that most owners have never seen, could not describe, and have never once had to remember to switch on.
